clue.text: Bold introduction to a meaningful piece of text

definitions.text: Bold introduction to a meaningful piece of text

blocks.note: surface reading: a daring opening to some significant writing
setter's reading: a dictionary entry, which gives a meaning and is introduced by its word printed in bold type

explanation.surface: A writer opens an important essay with a bold flourish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bold' sounds like daring, but it is the typeface; 'meaningful piece of text' is a dictionary entry.
explanation.definitionFit: In a dictionary each entry begins with the word being defined, printed in heavy type as its heading.

clue.text: Give what comes in a going-over?

definitions.text: Give what comes in a going-over?

indicators.note: going over means turning over, so the word is flipped end to end

blocks.note: the tide is what comes in, twice a day, at the shore

explanation.surface: An editor checks the copy that has just arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue is the job: giving incoming copy a once-over. Read cryptically, the incoming sea is turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: Copy arriving at a newspaper desk is checked and corrected before printing, which is revising it.

clue.text: Nag leading drink-driver?

blocks.note: surface reading: a motorist over the alcohol limit
setter's reading: a horse pulling the brewer's cart that delivers beer, with its carter behind

explanation.surface: Someone pesters a drunk motorist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nag' looks like a verb, to pester; it is a horse. A dray is a low cart for barrels, so its driver drives drink.
explanation.definitionFit: This heavy horse traditionally hauled a brewer's cart of beer barrels, so it walks ahead of the carter.

clue.text: Doesn't put out the port

indicators.note: something put out is disturbed or dislocated, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone declines to extinguish the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' tempts as wine, and 'doesn't put out' as a refusal; the six letters of the first word rearrange into a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostend is a Belgian harbour town on the North Sea, long a ferry crossing point from England.

clue.text: Fail to mention origins of Hengist and Horsa?

definitions.text: Fail to mention origins of Hengist and Horsa?

blocks.note: surface reading: the ancestry of the legendary brothers who led the Anglo-Saxon invasion of Britain

blocks.clueFragment: Fail to mention origins of Hengist and Horsa?
blocks.note: setter's reading: leaving out the letter both names begin with when speaking

explanation.surface: A historian skips over where the founders of Anglo-Saxon England came from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Origins' sounds genealogical; it means the initial letters, both H. Dropping that sound is a mark of Cockney speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes not pronouncing the H sound at the start of words, as in 'ouse for house.

clue.text: Booze with soldiers, after clique rejects outsiders

indicators.note: throwing away the outside letters of the word leaves only its interior
tells us the soldiers come behind the other piece in the answer

blocks.note: the word with its first and last letters dropped
OR, other ranks, the ordinary soldiers as opposed to officers

explanation.surface: Troops drinking with a gang that has thrown out the outsiders.
explanation.definitionFit: Booze is the informal word for alcoholic drink, and liquor is a general term for spirits and strong drink.

clue.text: A very hard Times crossword, one hears

blocks.note: first meaning: the notoriously difficult puzzle, then printed in The Times on Saturdays
second meaning: a person who hears

explanation.walkthrough: The Listener crossword began in the BBC's Listener magazine and moved to The Times in 1991.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle's name, taken from its old magazine, is also the plain word for someone paying attention to sounds.

clue.text: A couple of pints? Forgetting right time, two females drink a lot

indicators.note: what is forgotten is left out, so the named letters are dropped

blocks.note: a quart is two pints
R is the abbreviation for right
T is the abbreviation for time
F for female, twice

explanation.surface: A drinker, a couple of pints in, loses track of time and two women drink heavily.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking R and T out of QUART leaves QUA.
explanation.definitionFit: To quaff is to gulp down large draughts of a drink heartily.

clue.text: Twice, one pass spoiled ideal chance to shoot

indicators.note: something spoiled is ruined and disordered, so its letters are mixed up

blocks.note: the word one taken twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A footballer twice wastes a pass when a perfect shooting chance was there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' and 'pass' sound like football; the answer is the period when game may be hunted.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally the months when hunting a species is allowed; figuratively, a time when anyone may be attacked freely.

clue.text: Artist missing from Strauss radio broadcast, causing calamity

indicators.note: something missing from a set has been taken out of it, so these letters are removed
broadcast seed is scattered about, so the remaining letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: RA, Royal Academician, the standard abbreviation for an artist
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A radio broadcast of Strauss without its performer turns out badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one R and one A out of STRAUSS RADIO, then rearrange the ten letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disastrous brings about a catastrophe, so it is literally the cause of calamity.

clue.text: 'esitate to make a statement

indicators.note: the apostrophe marks a dropped opening letter, as in Cockney speech, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: HAVER, to dither or hesitate, said without its initial H

explanation.surface: A Cockney hesitates before saying something.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe shows 'hesitate' has lost its H; so must its synonym HAVER, a British word for dither.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to declare or assert something formally, which is a verb for stating.

clue.text: Pass on responsibility for Punch very rapidly

blocks.note: to hand over a duty is to pass it to someone else
a punch is delivered with a fist

explanation.surface: Someone shifts the blame for a blow onto another person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch' at the start of a word looks like the puppet or the magazine; it is just a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, usually about making money, describes gaining something quickly and in large amounts.

clue.text: I heard head collaring joker — who saw it?

indicators.note: what is heard is a sound, so the pronoun is replaced by a word sounding the same
a collar fits snugly against the neck, so the head sits right against the joker

blocks.note: the pronoun and the organ of sight are pronounced alike
a wit is a joker
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A police officer seizes a prankster and asks who saw what happened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collaring' suggests one piece goes round the other, but here the headland is simply attached after the joker; a ness is a headland, as in Sheerness.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyewitness is a person who personally saw an event, the one asked to report what happened.

clue.text: One who practises putting on a green, for example

definitions.text: One who practises putting on a green, for example

blocks.note: surface reading: a golfer practising putts on the green

blocks.clueFragment: One who practises putting on a green, for example
blocks.note: setter's reading: a tradesman whose job is applying colours, green being one, to cloth

explanation.surface: A golfer works on short putts on the green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Practises putting' reads as golf; here 'practises' means works at a trade and a green is a colour applied.
explanation.definitionFit: This tradesman colours fabric, so applying a shade such as green is the work of the trade.

clue.text: Free to play about, neither finishes — a typical case

indicators.note: neither of the two words gets to finish, so each loses its final letter

blocks.note: exempt means free from an obligation
to lark is to fool about

explanation.surface: Someone released to fool around, though never quite finishing, is a typical example.
explanation.walkthrough: EXEMPT loses its T and LARK its K.
explanation.definitionFit: An exemplar is a model or representative instance, the standard specimen of its kind.

clue.text: Pizza topping? Go for every possible one!

blocks.note: go as energy or vigour
per means for each
on as feasible, as in 'that's not on'
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Choosing pizza toppings, someone urges trying every one available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go for' looks like a phrasal verb; it splits into 'Go' and 'for every'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepperoni is a spicy salami sliced and spread over pizzas, one of the commonest toppings.

clue.text: Professional loss adjuster offering revised view

definitions.text: Professional loss adjuster offering revised view

blocks.note: surface reading: an insurance assessor who reviews a claim

blocks.clueFragment: Professional loss adjuster offering revised view
blocks.note: setter's reading: a specialist who corrects failing eyesight and so lets one see differently

explanation.surface: An insurance assessor comes back with a reconsidered opinion on a claim.
explanation.walkthrough: A loss adjuster is an insurance assessor; here the loss is of sight, and the adjustment is with lenses.
explanation.definitionFit: This professional tests eyesight and prescribes glasses, correcting poor vision so the world looks sharper.

clue.text: On final course, exercises given to a climber

blocks.note: the sweet is the dessert, the last course of a meal
PE, physical education
taken as written

explanation.surface: On the last lap, a mountaineer is put through physical training.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final course' sounds like the home stretch of a race; it is pudding. The climber is a plant, not a mountaineer.
explanation.definitionFit: This fragrant garden plant climbs trellises and canes using tendrils, so it is a climbing plant.

clue.text: Screw forward, going into the pack

blocks.note: first meaning: a propeller, or airscrew, in its short form
second meaning: a rugby forward on either side of the front row of the scrum

explanation.surface: A bolt pushed forward into a bundle.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the pack is the eight forwards who bind together in the scrum; the two props sit at its front corners.
explanation.definitionFit: The short word means both an aircraft or ship propeller and a front-row rugby player.

clue.text: Nasty graze beginning to bleed in recent war-zone

indicators.note: a nasty wound is a mess, so the letters come out jumbled
the beginning of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bad scrape starts to bleed in a battle zone.
explanation.definitionFit: Croatia's capital came under attack in the early 1990s Yugoslav wars, recent fighting when this puzzle ran.

clue.text: What's in store for one sort of car in traffic?

blocks.note: a stock car is one kind of car, raced on oval tracks
taken as written
traffic as dealing in goods, as in drug traffic

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what fate awaits a particular car stuck in a jam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's in store' sounds like what the future holds, but it means the goods a shop keeps; 'traffic' is commerce, not cars.
explanation.definitionFit: A business's stock-in-trade is its goods on hand, literally the merchandise kept in a shop.

clue.text: Some interest in Channel Islands, . and one in the Med

indicators.note: the interest sits inside the islands, so those letters are placed within the other abbreviation

blocks.note: CI, the standard abbreviation for the Channel Islands
APR, annual percentage rate, a measure of interest charged

explanation.surface: Someone has investments in Jersey and Guernsey and a holiday home in the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands are British islands near France, popular for offshore money. The page has a stray dot before 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is an island in the Bay of Naples, part of the Mediterranean Sea.

clue.text: The beak reveals the charge

blocks.note: first meaning: a bird's horny mouthparts
second meaning: the amount asked for payment

explanation.surface: A magistrate announces what the accused is charged with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beak' is British slang for a magistrate and 'charge' sounds like an accusation, but they are a bird's mouth and a price.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a bird's mouthparts and an invoice listing the money owed.

clue.text: Jack replaces front part to maintain vehicle

indicators.note: says the opening letter of the word is swapped out for another one

blocks.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack
to keep something is to maintain it

explanation.surface: A mechanic uses a jack and swaps a front part to service a car.
explanation.walkthrough: The K at the front of KEEP gives way to J.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeep is a sturdy four-wheel-drive car first built for military use, a kind of motor vehicle.

clue.text: Sounding out new damage found in order from Greece

indicators.note: things found in a place are inside it, so these letters sit within the other word

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
to harm is to damage
Ionic is one of the classical orders of Greek architecture

explanation.surface: Investigating fresh harm turned up by an instruction from Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounding out' looks like probing; it means sounding out of tune. The 'order' is architectural, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inharmonic is discordant, so its notes sound out of tune with one another.

clue.text: To dish out caning is said to be somewhat retrogressive

indicators.note: somewhat means only a part, so the letters are a piece taken from inside the words
something retrogressive goes backwards, so the run of letters is read from right to left

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of caning, all of is, and the start of said

explanation.surface: A remark that giving out corporal punishment is a backward practice.
explanation.definitionFit: To assign is to allot or allocate, which is to hand out shares or tasks to people.

clue.text: A foreign film script

blocks.note: surface reading: the screenplay of a film made abroad
setter's reading: the translated words printed along the bottom of the screen for a foreign-language film

explanation.surface: The screenplay of an overseas film.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'script' sounds like the screenplay; it is the written text shown on screen.
explanation.definitionFit: Translated captions appear at the foot of the picture so viewers can follow dialogue in another language.
